agent: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, this repository) — GUIDED execution policy
summary_for_principal:
You asked whether the engine handles both of the format's two run modes: STRICT, where nothing gets skipped, and GUIDED, where a person can skip a minor step. It only handled STRICT — GUIDED had been described in the format's own rulebook since the very first work package, but nothing in the engine ever acted on it. Built the missing half: under GUIDED, someone holding the right permission can now skip a step marked as low-stakes, and must record why; a step marked standard or critical can never be skipped, whatever the mode. Proven with six new tests, each checking one way the engine must refuse a skip it shouldn't allow. One design choice made along the way: the engine doesn't itself stop and offer a skip before every low-stakes step — a caller decides to invoke it, or doesn't, and the run proceeds normally either way. While in this code, fixed one small, already-broken thing next to it: a decision-maker's recorded reason for a gate decision was accepted but silently thrown away; it's now kept. Found two related gaps I did not fix, to keep this change to one concern: a gate's note isn't yet copied into the run's own memory the way one worked example shows, and a policy-based decision's reasoning isn't yet kept alongside its evidence. Both recorded for later.

1. The priority question from two reports ago is still open and still yours: build out the missing pieces (parallel work, loops over lists, one process calling another), wire in a real AI model for the steps this engine currently only pauses on, or something else.

decisions.headline: D15: a step is only skippable when it declares skip_permission; the engine refuses skip() otherwise, even under GUIDED with a TRIVIAL step.
decisions.problem: S6 says "a person with permission MAY skip a step whose criticality is TRIVIAL" but, like the gate/tool/process permission gaps closed earlier in this work package (D12-D14), never names which permission string governs that specific action — so the engine has nothing to authorize() against unless the definition itself supplies one.
options_rejected: Use the step's own permission field (if any) that already gates other actions on it: rejected — conflates "who may cause this step to run/dispatch" with "who may cause this step to be skipped", two different authorizations a process author may legitimately want to grant to different roles.

Fall back to a process-level default skip permission: rejected — invents a convention not in the spec; S15 already holds the one place defaults are allowed to live, and adding a second default location there wasn't asked for and isn't needed to make skip() work.

Allow skip whenever GUIDED + TRIVIAL, with no permission field at all: rejected — violates "permission first" (nothing runs, dispatches, or decides without an authorization call) and fail-closed; a TRIVIAL step is still a real action being skipped.
decisions.cost_to_change: Localized to one optional StepNode field, one schema property, and the guard clause in skip(); no migration needed since older definitions simply have skip_permission absent and are correctly refused if anyone calls skip() on them.

evidence.claim: S6's own text describes the permission-gated skip but names no field; the same gap shape recurred at D12 (Tool dispatch), D13 (gate decision with no deciders), D14 (run start).
evidence.source: docs/spec/process-definition.md S6 and S18, read directly this session and across the prior three fixes in this work package.

evidence.claim: skip() refuses independently on each of: node not STEP, process not GUIDED, criticality not TRIVIAL, skip_permission absent, no reason given, and authorize() returning anything but PERMIT.
evidence.source: tests/engine/test_run.py — six new tests, one per condition, each constructed so only the one condition under test is unmet.

decisions.revisit_if: A future work package asks for role-scoped skip authorities that differ from a step's dispatch authority in some more granular way (e.g. per-reason-category permissions) — not requested now.

decisions.headline: skip() is a proactive action a caller may invoke before a step's first attempt; next() does not itself pause or offer a skip before a TRIVIAL step.
decisions.problem: S6 describes what happens when a step IS skipped, but not the interaction flow — whether the engine must stop and present skip as an option before every TRIVIAL step under GUIDED, or whether skip is simply available on request.
options_rejected: Have next() pause and hand off before every TRIVIAL step under GUIDED, offering skip as a choice alongside normal dispatch: rejected — the engine's whole run-state is reconstructed by replaying durable AttemptRecords (S12.1: nothing held in memory between calls); a forced pause with no attempt yet recorded has nothing to replay from and would need new durable state invented for this one purpose, which S6 does not ask for and which would widen this change well beyond "support GUIDED".
decisions.cost_to_change: If a future spec revision mandates a forced offer-to-skip pause, that is new durable state and a new NextAnswer shape — additive, not a rewrite of skip() itself.

evidence.claim: next()'s NextAnswer already carries a new skippable flag (true exactly when _is_skippable(process, node) holds) so a caller building a UI can offer the choice without the engine forcing a pause.
evidence.source: src/sulis_workflows/engine/run.py — NextAnswer.skippable, set at the TOOL_STEP hand-off.

decisions.revisit_if: S6 or a later spec revision is amended to require the engine itself to withhold dispatch until skip is explicitly declined — not currently written.

lessons.maxim: When a spec describes an action gated "by a person with permission" but the surrounding prose names no field, check whether the same gap shape has already recurred elsewhere in the same spec (D12-D14 here) before designing the fix — the repeated shape is itself evidence for which fix pattern to reuse, rather than inventing a new one.
lessons.incident: GUIDED's skip permission is the fourth instance in this work package of "prose names a permission-gated action, no field names which permission" (Tool dispatch, gate-with-no-deciders, run start, now skip) — resolving it identically (an optional field, fail closed when absent, a new decision-log entry with the same shape) kept the fix predictable and the spec's own conventions internally consistent, rather than each instance getting a bespoke resolution.
lessons.destination: Any future permission-gap found in this spec: check S18's decision log for D12-D15 first: same shape, same fix.

ready_now: GUIDED execution policy and STRICT are both implemented and tested; a process author can now write execution_policy: GUIDED with per-step criticality and skip_permission and have the engine enforce it correctly in both directions (permits when it should, refuses when it shouldn't).
